You are implementing ONE requirement in the Apache Hadoop source tree at /workspace (a real upstream repo checked out at an earlier state).

REQUIREMENT SLUG: outputstream-md-typos
REQUIREMENT FILE: /workspace/requirements/outputstream-md-typos.yaml   <-- READ THIS FIRST

The `title:` field names the real upstream Apache Hadoop JIRA / git commit. Your job is to reproduce that upstream change as faithfully as you can from the requirement text plus the code you find in the tree. Hidden tests derived from the real upstream commit will grade the result, so EXACT naming matters:
  * new/changed configuration keys and their default values (and their entries in *-default.xml)
  * new class / interface / method / field / metric names and their visibility
  * log message wording and format placeholders
  * behavioural details (return values, exception types, ordering, off-by-one boundaries)
If the requirement text names an identifier (class, method, config key, metric, constant), use that identifier verbatim.

HOW TO WORK
1. Read the requirement yaml. Note the JIRA id and the module it belongs to (HDFS / YARN / MAPREDUCE / HADOOP-common / tools).
2. Locate the real code with Grep/Glob. Read enough surrounding code (and the existing tests for it) to make a correct, idiomatic change.
3. Implement the change. Match the surrounding code style, license headers, checkstyle habits (2-space indent, 80-col-ish, final where used, LOG placeholders `{}`).
4. If the change adds a config key, also add it to the matching `*-default.xml` (hdfs-default.xml / core-default.xml / yarn-default.xml / mapred-default.xml) with a sensible description, and to the `DFSConfigKeys`/`YarnConfiguration`/etc. constants class the module uses. Some modules have a TestYarnConfigurationFields / TestHdfsConfigFields style test that requires the xml and the constant to agree - keep them in sync.
5. If the upstream change would have come with tests, add or extend the corresponding test class under the same module (src/test/java/...). Keep tests deterministic and cheap. Do not add tests that need network or a real cluster beyond the usual MiniDFSCluster/MiniYARNCluster idioms already used in that test file.
6. Do NOT run maven/mvn or cmake (there is no warm build environment; it wastes your time). Instead be rigorous by inspection: every symbol you reference must exist (grep to confirm), every new import must be needed and correct, braces/parens balanced, no stale references left behind. Re-read your own final diff (`git diff -- <your files>`) before finishing and fix anything sloppy.
7. Scope discipline: change ONLY what this requirement needs. Do not reformat unrelated lines, do not fix unrelated warnings, do not touch other subsystems. Other agents are concurrently implementing ~380 other requirements in this same working tree.

FORBIDDEN COMMANDS (they would destroy other agents' concurrent work): git checkout / switch / stash / reset / revert / clean / rebase / merge / cherry-pick, `git add -A` or `git add .` without an explicit pathspec, `git commit --amend`, `git rm` of files you did not create, and any `mvn`/`gradle` invocation.

WHEN YOUR IMPLEMENTATION IS COMPLETE - commit it yourself with exactly this shape (substitute the real repo-relative paths you touched, space separated, and keep the flock):

  cd /workspace && flock /tmp/hadoop-git.lock bash -c 'git add -A -- PATH1 PATH2 ... && git diff --cached --binary > requirement_patches/outputstream-md-typos.diff && git commit -q -m "impl: outputstream-md-typos" && git log --oneline -1 && wc -c requirement_patches/outputstream-md-typos.diff'

Rules for that step:
  * List every file you created, modified or deleted as an explicit pathspec. Never a bare directory like `.`.
  * requirement_patches/outputstream-md-typos.diff MUST come out non-empty (wc -c > 0). If `git commit` reports "nothing to commit", another agent already committed your lines: verify the requirement is genuinely satisfied in the working tree, then report that in your notes.
  * Do not touch requirement_patches/ for any other slug.

FINALLY return ONLY a JSON object (this is your return value, not a message to a human):
{"slug":"outputstream-md-typos","status":"done"|"partial"|"blocked","files":["..."],"committed":true|false,"patch_bytes":<int>,"summary":"<=3 sentences on what you changed","notes":"anything the orchestrator must know (conflicts, follow-ups, uncertainty)"}

1 14 15 16 17 # Output: `OutputStream`, `Syncable` and `StreamCapabilities` 18 19 ## Introduction 20 21 This document covers the Output Streams within the context of the 22 [Hadoop File System Specification](index.html). 23 24 It uses the filesystem model defined in [A Model of a Hadoop Filesystem](model.html) 25 with the notation defined in [notation](Notation.md). 26 27 The target audiences are: 28 1. Users of the APIs. While `java.io.OutputStream` is a standard interfaces, 29 this document clarifies how it is implemented in HDFS and elsewhere. 30 The Hadoop-specific interfaces `Syncable` and `StreamCapabilities` are new; 31 `Syncable` is notable in offering durability and visibility guarantees which 32 exceed that of `OutputStream`. 33 1. Implementors of File Systems and clients. 34 35 ## How data is written to a filesystem 36 37 The core mechanism to write data to files through the Hadoop FileSystem APIs 38 is through `OutputStream` subclasses obtained through calls to 39 `FileSystem.create()`, `FileSystem.append()`, 40 or `FSDataOutputStreamBuilder.build()`. 41 42 These all return instances of `FSDataOutputStream`, through which data 43 can be written through various `write()` methods. 44 After a stream's `close()` method is called, all data written to the 45 stream MUST BE persisted to the fileysystem and visible to oll other 46 clients attempting to read data from that path via `FileSystem.open()`. 47 48 As well as operations to write the data, Hadoop's `OutputStream` implementations 49 provide methods to flush buffered data back to the filesystem, 50 so as to ensure that the data is reliably persisted and/or visible 51 to other callers. This is done via the `Syncable` interface. It was 52 originally intended that the presence of this interface could be interpreted 53 as a guarantee that the stream supported its methods. However, this has proven 54 impossible to guarantee as the static nature of the interface is incompatible 55 with filesystems whose syncability semantics may vary on a store/path basis. 56 As an example, erasure coded files in HDFS do not support the Sync operations, 57 even though they are implemented as subclass of an output stream which is `Syncable`. 58 59 A new interface: `StreamCapabilities`. This allows callers 60 to probe the exact capabilities of a stream, even transitively 61 through a chain of streams. 62 63 ## Output Stream Model 64 65 For this specification, an output stream can be viewed as a list of bytes 66 stored in the client; `hsync()` and `hflush()` are operations the actions 67 which propagate the data to be visible to other readers of the file and/or 68 made durable. 69 70 ```python 71 buffer: List[byte] 72 ``` 73 74 A flag, `open` tracks whether the stream is open: after the stream 75 is closed no more data may be written to it: 76 77 ```python 78 open: bool 79 buffer: List[byte] 80 ``` 81 82 The destination path of the stream, `path`, can be tracked to form a triple 83 `path, open, buffer` 84 85 ```python 86 Stream = (path: Path, open: Boolean, buffer: byte[]) 87 ``` 88 89 #### Visibility of Flushed Data 90 91 (Immediately) after `Syncable` operations which flush data to the filesystem, 92 the data at the stream's destination path MUST match that of 93 `buffer`. That is, the following condition MUST hold: 94 95 ```python 96 FS'.Files(path) == buffer 97 ``` 98 99 Any client reading the data at the path MUST see the new data. 100 The `Syncable` operations differ in their durability 101 guarantees, not visibility of data. 102 103 ### State of Stream and File System after `Filesystem.create()` 104 105 The output stream returned by a `FileSystem.create(path)` or 106 `FileSystem.createFile(path).build()` within a filesystem `FS`, 107 can be modeled as a triple containing an empty array of no data: 108 109 ```python 110 Stream' = (path, true, []) 111 ``` 112 113 The filesystem `FS'` MUST contain a 0-byte file at the path: 114 115 ```python 116 FS' = FS where data(FS', path) == [] 117 ``` 118 119 Thus, the initial state of `Stream'.buffer` is implicitly 120 consistent with the data at the filesystem. 121 122 123 *Object Stores*: see caveats in the "Object Stores" section below. 124 125 ### State of Stream and File System after `Filesystem.append()` 126 127 The output stream returned from a call of 128 `FileSystem.append(path, buffersize, progress)` within a filesystem `FS`, 129 can be modelled as a stream whose `buffer` is intialized to that of 130 the original file: 131 132 ```python 133 Stream' = (path, true, data(FS, path)) 134 ``` 135 136 #### Persisting data 137 138 When the stream writes data back to its store, be it in any 139 supported flush operation, in the `close()` operation, or at any other 140 time the stream chooses to do so, the contents of the file 141 are replaced with the current buffer 142 143 ```python 144 Stream' = (path, true, buffer) 145 FS' = FS where data(FS', path) == buffer 146 ``` 147 148 After a call to `close()`, the stream is closed for all operations other 149 than `close()`; they MAY fail with `IOException` or `RuntimeException`. 150 151 ```python 152 Stream' = (path, false, []) 153 ``` 154 155 The `close()` operation MUST be idempotent with the sole attempt to write the 156 data made in the first invocation. 157 158 1. If `close()` succeeds, subsequent calls are no-ops. 159 1. If `close()` fails, again, subsequent calls are no-ops. They MAY rethrow 160 the previous exception, but they MUST NOT retry the write. 161 162 163 164 165 166 ## Class `FSDataOutputStream` 167 168 ```java 169 public class FSDataOutputStream 170 extends DataOutputStream 171 implements Syncable, CanSetDropBehind, StreamCapabilities { 172 // ... 173 } 174 ``` 175 176 The `FileSystem.create()`, `FileSystem.append()` and 177 `FSDataOutputStreamBuilder.build()` calls return an instance 178 of a class `FSDataOutputStream`, a subclass of `java.io.OutputStream`. 179 180 The base class wraps an `OutputStream` instance, one which may implement `Syncable`, 181 `CanSetDropBehind` and `StreamCapabilities`. 182 183 This document covers the requirements of such implementations. 184 185 HDFS's `FileSystem` implementation, `DistributedFileSystem`, returns an instance 186 of `HdfsDataOutputStream`. This implementation has at least two behaviors 187 which are not explicitly declared by the base Java implmentation 188 189 1. Writes are synchronized: more than one thread can write to the same 190 output stream. This is a use pattern which HBase relies on. 191 192 1. `OutputStream.flush()` is a no-op when the file is closed. Apache Druid 193 has made such a call on this in the past 194 [HADOOP-14346](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/HADOOP-14346). 195 196 197 As the HDFS implementation is considered the de-facto specification of 198 the FileSystem APIs, the fact that `write()` is thread-safe is significant. 199 200 For compatibility, not only SHOULD other FS clients be thread-safe, 201 but new HDFS features, such as encryption and Erasure Coding SHOULD also 202 implement consistent behavior with the core HDFS output stream. 203 204 Put differently: 205 206 *It isn't enough for Output Streams to implement the core semantics 207 of `java.io.OutputStream`: they need to implement the extra semantics 208 of `HdfsDataOutputStream`, especially for HBase to work correctly.* 209 210 The concurrent `write()` call is the most significant tightening of 211 the Java specification. 212 213 ## Class `java.io.OutputStream` 214 215 A Java `OutputStream` allows applications to write a sequence of bytes to a destination. 216 In a Hadoop filesystem, that destination is the data under a path in the filesystem. 217 218 ```java 219 public abstract class OutputStream implements Closeable, Flushable { 220 public abstract void write(int b) throws IOException; 221 public void write(byte b[]) throws IOException; 222 public void write(byte b[], int off, int len) throws IOException; 223 public void flush() throws IOException; 224 public void close() throws IOException; 225 } 226 ``` 227 ### `write(Stream, data)` 228 229 Writes a byte of data to the stream. 230 231 #### Preconditions 232 233 ```python 234 Stream.open else raise ClosedChannelException, PathIOException, IOException 235 ``` 236 237 The exception `java.nio.channels.ClosedChannelExceptionn` is 238 raised in the HDFS output streams when trying to write to a closed file. 239 This exception does not include the destination path; and 240 `Exception.getMessage()` is `null`. It is therefore of limited value in stack 241 traces. Implementors may wish to raise exceptions with more detail, such 242 as a `PathIOException`. 243 244 245 #### Postconditions 246 247 The buffer has the lower 8 bits of the data argument appended to it. 248 249 ```python 250 Stream'.buffer = Stream.buffer + [data & 0xff] 251 ``` 252 253 There may be an explicit limit on the size of cached data, or an implicit 254 limit based by the available capacity of the destination filesystem. 255 When a limit is reached, `write()` SHOULD fail with an `IOException`. 256 257 ### `write(Stream, byte[] data, int offset, int len)` 258 259 260 #### Preconditions 261 262 The preconditions are all defined in `OutputStream.write()` 263 264 ```python 265 Stream.open else raise ClosedChannelException, PathIOException, IOException 266 data != null else raise NullPointerException 267 offset >= 0 else raise IndexOutOfBoundsException 268 len >= 0 else raise IndexOutOfBoundsException 269 offset < data.length else raise IndexOutOfBoundsException 270 offset + len < data.length else raise IndexOutOfBoundsException 271 ``` 272 273 After the operation has returned, the buffer may be re-used. The outcome 274 of updates to the buffer while the `write()` operation is in progress is undefined. 275 276 #### Postconditions 277 278 ```python 279 Stream'.buffer = Stream.buffer + data[offset...(offset + len)] 280 ``` 281 282 ### `write(byte[] data)` 283 284 This is defined as the equivalent of: 285 286 ```python 287 write(data, 0, data.length) 288 ``` 289 290 ### `flush()` 291 292 Requests that the data is flushed. The specification of `ObjectStream.flush()` 293 declares that this SHOULD write data to the "intended destination". 294 295 It explicitly precludes any guarantees about durability. 296 297 For that reason, this document doesn't provide any normative 298 specifications of behaviour. 299 300 #### Preconditions 301 302 None. 303 304 #### Postconditions 305 306 None. 307 308 If the implementation chooses to implement a stream-flushing operation, 309 the data may be saved to the file system such that it becomes visible to 310 others" 311 312 ```python 313 FS' = FS where data(FS', path) == buffer 314 ``` 315 316 When a stream is closed, `flush()` SHOULD downgrade to being a no-op, if it was not 317 one already. This is to work with applications and libraries which can invoke 318 it in exactly this way. 319 320 321 *Issue*: Should `flush()` forward to `hflush()`? 322 323 No. Or at least, make it optional. 324 325 There's a lot of application code which assumes that `flush()` is low cost 326 and should be invoked after writing every single line of output, after 327 writing small 4KB blocks or similar. 328 329 Forwarding this to a full flush across a distributed filesystem, or worse, 330 a distant object store, is very inefficient. 331 Filesystem clients which convert a `flush()` to an `hflush()` will eventually 332 have to roll back that feature: 333 [HADOOP-16548](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/HADOOP-16548). 334 335 ### `close()` 336 337 The `close()` operation saves all data to the filesystem and 338 releases any resources used for writing data. 339 340 The `close()` call is expected to block 341 until the write has completed (as with `Syncable.hflush()`), possibly 342 until it has been written to durable storage. 343 344 After `close()` completes, the data in a file MUST be visible and consistent 345 with the data most recently written. The metadata of the file MUST be consistent 346 with the data and the write history itself (i.e. any modification time fields 347 updated). 348 349 After `close()` is invoked, all subsequent `write()` calls on the stream 350 MUST fail with an `IOException`. 351 352 Any locking/leaseholding mechanism MUST release its lock/lease. 353 354 ```python 355 Stream'.open = false 356 FS' = FS where data(FS', path) == buffer 357 ``` 358 359 The `close()` call MAY fail during its operation. 360 361 1. Callers of the API MUST expect for some calls to `close()` to fail and SHOULD code appropriately. 362 Catching and swallowing exceptions, while common, is not always the ideal solution. 363 1. Even after a failure, `close()` MUST place the stream into a closed state. 364 Follow-on calls to `close()` are ignored, and calls to other methods 365 rejected. That is: caller's cannot be expected to call `close()` repeatedly 366 until it succeeds. 367 1. The duration of the `close()` operation is undefined. Operations which rely 368 on acknowledgements from remote systems to meet the persistence guarantees 369 implicitly have to await these acknowledgements. Some Object Store output streams 370 upload the entire data file in the `close()` operation. This can take a large amount 371 of time. The fact that many user applications assume that `close()` is both fast 372 and does not fail means that this behavior is dangerous. 373 374 Recommendations for safe use by callers 375 376 * Do plan for exceptions being raised, either in catching and logging or 377 by throwing the exception further up. Catching and silently swallowing exceptions 378 may hide serious problems. 379 * Heartbeat operations SHOULD take place on a separate thread, so that a long 380 delay in `close()` does not block the thread so long that the heartbeat times 381 out. 382 383 Implementors: 384 385 * Have a look at [HADOOP-16785](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/HADOOP-16785) 386 to see examples of complications in close. 387 * Incrementally writing blocks before a close operation results in a behavior which 388 matches client expectations better: write failures to surface earlier and close 389 to be more housekeeping than the actual upload. 390 * If block uploads are executed in separate threads, the output stream `close()` 391 call MUST block until all the asynchronous uploads have completed; any error raised 392 MUST be reported. 393 If multiple errors were raised, the stream can choose which to propagate. 394 What is important is: when `close()` returns without an error, applications expect 395 the data to have been successfully written. 396 397 ### HDFS and `OutputStream.close()` 398 399 HDFS does not immediately `sync()` the output of a written file to disk on 400 `OutputStream.close()` unless configured with `dfs.datanode.synconclose` 401 is true. This has caused [problems in some applications](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/ACCUMULO-1364). 402 403 Applications which absolutely require the guarantee that a file has been persisted 404 MUST call `Syncable.hsync()` *before* the file is closed. 405 406 407 ## `org.apache.hadoop.fs.Syncable` 408 409 ```java 410 @InterfaceAudience.Public 411 @InterfaceStability.Stable 412 public interface Syncable { 413 414 415 /** Flush out the data in client's user buffer. After the return of 416 * this call, new readers will see the data. 417 * @throws IOException if any error occurs 418 */ 419 void hflush() throws IOException; 420 421 /** Similar to posix fsync, flush out the data in client's user buffer 422 * all the way to the disk device (but the disk may have it in its cache). 423 * @throws IOException if error occurs 424 */ 425 void hsync() throws IOException; 426 } 427 ``` 428 429 The purpose of `Syncable` interface is to provide guarantees that data is written 430 to a filesystem for both visibility and durability. 431 432 *SYNC-1*: An `OutputStream` which implements `Syncable` and does not raise 433 `UnsupportedOperationException` on invocations is 434 making an explicit declaration that it can meet those guarantees. 435 436 *SYNC-2*: If a stream, declares the interface as implemented, but does not 437 provide durability, the interface's methods MUST raise 438 `UnsupportedOperationException`. 439 440 The `Syncable` interface has been implemented by other classes than 441 subclasses of `OutputStream`, such as `org.apache.hadoop.io.SequenceFile.Writer`. 442 443 *SYNC-3* The fact that a class implements `Syncable` does not guarantee 444 that `extends OutputStream` holds. 445 446 That is, for any class `C`: `(C instanceof Syncable)` does not imply 447 `(C instanceof OutputStream)` 448 449 This specification only covers the required behavior of `OutputStream` subclasses 450 which implement `Syncable`. 451 452 453 *SYNC-4:* The return value of `FileSystem.create(Path)` is an instance 454 of `FSDataOutputStream`. 455 456 *SYNC-5:* `FSDataOutputStream implements Syncable` 457 458 459 SYNC-5 and SYNC-1 imply that all output streams which can be created 460 with `FileSystem.create(Path)` must support the semantics of `Syncable`. 461 This is demonstrably not true: `FSDataOutputStream` simply downgrades 462 to a `flush()` if its wrapped stream is not `Syncable`. 463 Therefore the declarations SYNC-1 and SYNC-2 do not hold: you cannot trust `Syncable`. 464 465 Put differently: *callers MUST NOT rely on the presence of the interface 466 as evidence that the semantics of `Syncable` are supported*. Instead 467 they MUST be dynamically probed for using the `StreamCapabilities` 468 interface, where available. 469 470 471 ### `Syncable.hflush()` 472 473 Flush out the data in client's user buffer. After the return of 474 this call, new readers will see the data. The `hflush()` operation 475 does not contain any guarantees as to the durability of the data. only 476 its visibility. 477 478 Thus implementations may cache the written data in memory 479 —visible to all, but not yet persisted. 480 481 #### Preconditions 482 483 ```python 484 hasCapability(Stream, "hflush") 485 Stream.open else raise IOException 486 ``` 487 488 489 #### Postconditions 490 491 ```python 492 FS' = FS where data(path) == cache 493 ``` 494 495 496 After the call returns, the data MUST be visible to all new callers 497 of `FileSystem.open(path)` and `FileSystem.openFile(path).build()`. 498 499 There is no requirement or guarantee that clients with an existing 500 `DataInputStream` created by a call to `(FS, path)` will see the updated 501 data, nor is there a guarantee that they *will not* in a current or subsequent 502 read. 503 504 Implementation note: as a correct `hsync()` implementation MUST also 505 offer all the semantics of an `hflush()` call, implementations of `hflush()` 506 may just invoke `hsync()`: 507 508 ```java 509 public void hflush() throws IOException { 510 hsync(); 511 } 512 ``` 513 514 #### `hflush()` Performance 515 516 The `hflush()` call MUST block until the store has acknowledge that the 517 data has been received and is now visible to others. This can be slow, 518 as it will include the time to upload any outstanding data from the 519 client, and for the filesystem itself to process it. 520 521 Often Filesystems only offer the `Syncable.hsync()` guarantees: persistence as 522 well as visibility. This means the time to return can be even greater. 523 524 Application code MUST NOT call `hflush()` or `hsync()` at the end of every line 525 or, unless they are writing a WAL, at the end of every record. Use with care. 526 527 528 ### `Syncable.hsync()` 529 530 Similar to POSIX `fsync()`, this call saves the data in client's user buffer 531 all the way to the disk device (but the disk may have it in its cache). 532 533 That is: it is a requirement for the underlying FS To save all the data to 534 the disk hardware itself, where it is expected to be durable. 535 536 #### Preconditions 537 538 ```python 539 hasCapability(Stream, "hsync") 540 Stream.open else raise IOException 541 ``` 542 543 #### Postconditions 544 545 ```python 546 FS' = FS where data(path) == buffer 547 ``` 548 549 _Implementations are required to block until that write has been 550 acknowledged by the store._ 551 552 This is so the caller can be confident that once the call has 553 returned successfully, the data has been written. 554 555 556 557 ## Interface `StreamCapabilities` 558 559 ```java 560 @InterfaceAudience.Public 561 @InterfaceStability.Evolving 562 ``` 563 564 The `org.apache.hadoop.fs.StreamCapabilities` interface exists to allow callers to dynamically 565 determine the behavior of a stream. 566 567 ```java 568 public boolean hasCapability(String capability) { 569 switch (capability.toLowerCase(Locale.ENGLISH)) { 570 case StreamCapabilities.HSYNC: 571 case StreamCapabilities.HFLUSH: 572 return supportFlush; 573 default: 574 return false; 575 } 576 } 577 ``` 578 579 Once a stream has been closed, a `hasCapability()` call MUST do one of 580 581 * return the capabilities of the open stream. 582 * return false. 583 584 That is: it MUST NOT raise an exception about the file being closed; 585 586 See [pathcapabilities](pathcapabilities.html) for specifics on the `PathCapabilities` API; 587 the requirements are similar: a stream MUST NOT return true for a capability 588 for which it lacks support, be it because 589 590 * The capability is unknown. 591 * The capability is known and known to be unsupported. 592 593 Standard stream capabilities are defined in `StreamCapabilities`; 594 consult the javadocs for the complete set of options. 595 596 | Name | Probes for support of | 597 |-------|---------| 598 | `dropbehind` | `CanSetDropBehind.setDropBehind()` | 599 | `hsync` | `Syncable.hsync()` | 600 | `hflush` | `Syncable.hflush()`. Deprecated: probe for `HSYNC` only. | 601 | `in:readahead` | `CanSetReadahead.setReadahead()` | 602 | `in:unbuffer"` | `CanUnbuffer.unbuffer()` | 603 | `in:readbytebuffer` | `ByteBufferReadable#read(ByteBuffer)` | 604 | `in:preadbytebuffer` | `ByteBufferPositionedReadable#read(long, ByteBuffer)` | 605 606 Stream implementations MAY add their own custom options. 607 These MUST be prefixed with `fs.SCHEMA.`, where `SCHEMA` is the schema of the filesystem. 608 609 ## interface `CanSetDropBehind` 610 611 ```java 612 @InterfaceAudience.Public 613 @InterfaceStability.Evolving 614 public interface CanSetDropBehind { 615 /** 616 * Configure whether the stream should drop the cache. 617 * 618 * @param dropCache Whether to drop the cache. null means to use the 619 * default value. 620 * @throws IOException If there was an error changing the dropBehind 621 * setting. 622 * UnsupportedOperationException If this stream doesn't support 623 * setting the drop-behind. 624 */ 625 void setDropBehind(Boolean dropCache) 626 throws IOException, UnsupportedOperationException; 627 } 628 ``` 629 630 This interface allows callers to change policies used inside HDFS. 631 632 Implementations MUST return `true` for the call 633 634 ```java 635 StreamCapabilities.hasCapability("dropbehind"); 636 ``` 637 638 639 ## Durability, Concurrency, Consistency and Visibility of stream output. 640 641 These are the aspects of the system behaviour which are not directly 642 covered in this (very simplistic) filesystem model, but which are visible 643 in production. 644 645 646 ### Durability 647 648 1. `OutputStream.write()` MAY persist the data, synchronously or asynchronously 649 1. `OutputStream.flush()` flushes data to the destination. There 650 are no strict persistence requirements. 651 1. `Syncable.hflush()` synchronously sends all outstaning data to the destination 652 filesystem. After returning to the caller, the data MUST be visible to other readers, 653 it MAY be durable. That is: it does not have to be persisted, merely guaranteed 654 to be consistently visible to all clients attempting to open a new stream reading 655 data at the path. 656 1. `Syncable.hsync()` MUST transmit the data as per `hflush` and persist 657 that data to the underlying durable storage. 658 1. `close()` The first call to `close()` MUST flush out all remaining data in 659 the buffers, and persist it, as a call to `hsync()`. 660 661 662 Many applications call `flush()` far too often -such as at the end of every line written. 663 If this triggered an update of the data in persistent storage and any accompanying 664 metadata, distributed stores would overload fast. 665 Thus: `flush()` is often treated at most as a cue to flush data to the network 666 buffers -but not commit to writing any data. 667 668 It is only the `Syncable` interface which offers guarantees. 669 670 The two `Syncable` operations `hsync()` and `hflush()` differ purely by the extra guarantee of `hsync()`: the data must be persisted. 671 If `hsync()` is implemented, then `hflush()` can be implemented simply 672 by invoking `hsync()` 673 674 ```java 675 public void hflush() throws IOException { 676 hsync(); 677 } 678 ``` 679 680 This is perfectly acceptable as an implementation: the semantics of `hflush()` 681 are satisifed. 682 What is not acceptable is downgrading `hsync()` to `hflush()`, as the durability guarantee is no longer met. 683 684 685 ### Concurrency 686 687 1. The outcome of more than one process writing to the same file is undefined. 688 689 1. An input stream opened to read a file *before the file was opened for writing* 690 MAY fetch data updated by writes to an OutputStream. 691 Because of buffering and caching, this is not a requirement 692 —and if an input stream does pick up updated data, the point at 693 which the updated data is read is undefined. This surfaces in object stores 694 where a `seek()` call which closes and re-opens the connection may pick up 695 updated data, while forward stream reads do not. Similarly, in block-oriented 696 filesystems, the data may be cached a block at a time —and changes only picked 697 up when a different block is read. 698 699 1. A filesystem MAY allow the destination path to be manipulated while a stream 700 is writing to it —for example, `rename()` of the path or a parent; `delete()` of 701 a path or parent. In such a case, the outcome of future write operations on 702 the output stream is undefined. Some filesystems MAY implement locking to 703 prevent conflict. However, this tends to be rare on distributed filesystems, 704 for reasons well known in the literature. 705 706 1. The Java API specification of `java.io.OutputStream` does not require 707 an instance of the class to be thread safe. 708 However, `org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.DFSOutputStream` 709 has a stronger thread safety model (possibly unintentionally). This fact is 710 relied upon in Apache HBase, as discovered in HADOOP-11708. Implementations 711 SHOULD be thread safe. *Note*: even the `DFSOutputStream` synchronization 712 model permits the output stream to have `close()` invoked while awaiting an 713 acknowledgement from datanode or namenode writes in an `hsync()` operation. 714 715 ### Consistency and Visibility 716 717 There is no requirement for the data to be immediately visible to other applications 718 —not until a specific call to flush buffers or persist it to the underlying storage 719 medium are made. 720 721 If an output stream is created with `FileSystem.create(path, overwrite==true)` 722 and there is an existing file at the path, that is `exists(FS, path)` holds, 723 then, the existing data is immediately unavailable; the data at the end of the 724 path MUST consist of an empty byte sequence `[]`, with consistent metadata. 725 726 727 ```python 728 exists(FS, path) 729 (Stream', FS') = create(FS, path) 730 exists(FS', path) 731 getFileStatus(FS', path).getLen() = 0 732 ``` 733 734 The metadata of a file (`length(FS, path)` in particular) SHOULD be consistent 735 with the contents of the file after `flush()` and `sync()`. 736 737 ```python 738 (Stream', FS') = create(FS, path) 739 (Stream'', FS'') = write(Stream', data) 740 (Stream''', FS''') hsync(Stream'') 741 exists(FS''', path) 742 getFileStatus(FS''', path).getLen() = len(data) 743 ``` 744 745 *HDFS does not do this except when the write crosses a block boundary*; to do 746 otherwise would overload the Namenode. Other stores MAY copy this behavior. 747 748 As a result, while a file is being written 749 `length(Filesystem, Path)` MAY be less than the length of `data(Filesystem, Path)`. 750 751 The metadata MUST be consistent with the contents of a file after the `close()` 752 operation. 753 754 After the contents of an output stream have been persisted (`hflush()/hsync()`) 755 all new `open(FS, Path)` operations MUST return the updated data. 756 757 After `close()` has been invoked on an output stream, 758 a call to `getFileStatus(path)` MUST return the final metadata of the written file, 759 including length and modification time. 760 The metadata of the file returned in any of the FileSystem `list` operations 761 MUST be consistent with this metadata. 762 763 The value of `getFileStatus(path).getModificationTime()` is not defined 764 while a stream is being written to. 765 The timestamp MAY be updated while a file is being written, 766 especially after a `Syncable.hsync()` call. 767 The timestamps MUST be updated after the file is closed 768 to that of a clock value observed by the server during the `close()` call. 769 It is *likely* to be in the time and time zone of the filesystem, rather 770 than that of the client. 771 772 Formally, if a `close()` operation triggers an interaction with a server 773 which starts at server-side time `t1` and completes at time `t2` with a successfully 774 written file, then the last modification time SHOULD be a time `t` where 775 `t1 <= t <= t2` 776 777 ## Issues with the Hadoop Output Stream model. 778 779 There are some known issues with the output stream model as offered by Hadoop, 780 specifically about the guarantees about when data is written and persisted 781 —and when the metadata is synchronized. 782 These are where implementation aspects of HDFS and the "Local" filesystem 783 do not follow the simple model of the filesystem used in this specification. 784 785 ### HDFS 786 787 #### HDFS: `hsync()` only syncs the latest block 788 789 The reference implementation, `DFSOutputStream` will block until an 790 acknowledgement is received from the datanodes: that is, all hosts in the 791 replica write chain have successfully written the file. 792 793 That means that the expectation callers may have is that the return of the 794 method call contains visibility and durability guarantees which other 795 implementations must maintain. 796 797 Note, however, that the reference `DFSOutputStream.hsync()` call only actually 798 persists *the current block*. If there have been a series of writes since the 799 last sync, such that a block boundary has been crossed. The `hsync()` call 800 claims only to write the most recent. 801 802 From the javadocs of `DFSOutputStream.hsync(EnumSet syncFlags)` 803 804 > Note that only the current block is flushed to the disk device. 805 > To guarantee durable sync across block boundaries the stream should 806 > be created with {@link CreateFlag#SYNC_BLOCK}. 807 808 809 This is an important HDFS implementation detail which must not be ignored by 810 anyone relying on HDFS to provide a Write-Ahead-Log or other database structure 811 where the requirement of the application is that 812 "all preceeding bytes MUST have been persisted before the commit flag in the WAL 813 is flushed" 814 815 See [Stonebraker81], Michael Stonebraker, _Operating System Support for Database Management_, 816 1981, for a discussion on this topic. 817 818 If you do need `hsync()` to have synced every block in a very large write, call 819 it regularly. 820 821 #### HDFS: delayed visibility of metadata updates. 822 823 That HDFS file metadata often lags the content of a file being written 824 to is not something everyone expects, nor convenient for any program trying 825 to pick up updated data in a file being written. Most visible is the length 826 of a file returned in the various `list` commands and `getFileStatus` —this 827 is often out of date. 828 829 As HDFS only supports file growth in its output operations, this means 830 that the size of the file as listed in the metadata may be less than or equal 831 to the number of available bytes —but never larger. This is a guarantee which 832 is also held 833 834 One algorithm to determine whether a file in HDFS is updated is: 835 836 1. Remember the last read position `pos` in the file, using `0` if this is the initial 837 read. 838 1. Use `getFileStatus(FS, Path)` to query the updated length of the file as 839 recorded in the metadata. 840 1. If `Status.length > pos`, the file has grown. 841 1. If the number has not changed, then 842 1. Reopen the file. 843 1. `seek(pos)` to that location 844 1. If `read() != -1`, there is new data. 845 846 This algorithm works for filesystems which are consistent with metadata and 847 data, as well as HDFS. What is important to know is that, for an open file 848 `getFileStatus(FS, path).getLen() == 0` does not imply that `data(FS, path)` is 849 empty. 850 851 When an output stream in HDFS is closed; the newly written data is not immediately 852 written to disk unless HDFS is deployed with `dfs.datanode.synconclose` set to 853 true. Otherwise it is cached and written to disk later. 854 855 ### Local Filesystem, `file:` 856 857 `LocalFileSystem`, `file:`, (or any other `FileSystem` implementation based on 858 `ChecksumFileSystem`) has a different issue. If an output stream 859 is obtained from `create()` and `FileSystem.setWriteChecksum(false)` has 860 *not* been called on the filesystem, then the stream only flushes as much 861 local data as can be written to full checksummed blocks of data. 862 863 That is, the hsync/hflush operations are not guaranteed to write all the pending 864 data until the file is finally closed. 865 866 For this reason, the local fileystem accessed via `file://` URLs 867 does not support `Syncable` unless `setWriteChecksum(false)` was 868 called on that FileSystem instance so as to disable checksum creation. 869 After which, obviously, checksums are not generated for any file. 870 Is 871 ### Checksummed output streams 872 873 Because `org.apache.hadoop.fs.FSOutputSummer` and 874 `org.apache.hadoop.fs.ChecksumFileSystem.ChecksumFSOutputSummer` 875 implement the underlying checksummed output stream used by HDFS and 876 other filesystems, it provides some of the core semantics of the output 877 stream behavior. 878 879 1. The `close()` call is unsynchronized, re-entrant and may attempt 880 to close the stream more than once. 881 1. It is possible to call `write(int)` on a closed stream (but not 882 `write(byte[], int, int)`). 883 1. It is possible to call `flush()` on a closed stream. 884 885 Behaviors 1 and 2 really have to be considered bugs to fix, albeit with care. 886 887 Behavior 3 has to be considered a defacto standard, for other implementations 888 to copy. 889 890 ### Object Stores 891 892 Object store streams MAY buffer the entire stream's output 893 until the final `close()` operation triggers a single `PUT` of the data 894 and materialization of the final output. 895 896 This significantly changes their behaviour compared to that of 897 POSIX filesystems and that specified in this document. 898 899 #### Visibility of newly created objects 900 901 There is no guarantee that any file will be visible at the path of an output 902 stream after the output stream is created . 903 904 That is: while `create(FS, path, boolean)` returns a new stream 905 906 ```python 907 Stream' = (path, true, []) 908 ``` 909 910 The other postcondition of the operation, `data(FS', path) == []` MAY NOT 911 hold, in which case: 912 913 1. `exists(FS, p)` MAY return false. 914 1. If a file was created with `overwrite = True`, the existing data MAY still 915 be visible: `data(FS', path) = data(FS, path)`. 916 917 1. The check for existing data in a `create()` call with `overwrite=False`, may 918 take place in the `create()` call itself, in the `close()` call prior to/during 919 the write, or at some point in between. In the special case that the 920 object store supports an atomic `PUT` operation, the check for existence of 921 existing data and the subsequent creation of data at the path contains a race 922 condition: other clients may create data at the path between the existence check 923 and the subsequent write. 924 925 1. Calls to `create(FS, Path, overwrite=false)` MAY succeed, returning a new 926 `OutputStream`, even while another stream is open and writing to the destination 927 path. 928 929 This allows for the following sequence of operations, which would 930 raise an exception in the second `open()` call if invoked against HDFS: 931 932 ```python 933 Stream1 = open(FS, path, false) 934 sleep(200) 935 Stream2 = open(FS, path, false) 936 Stream.write('a') 937 Stream1.close() 938 Stream2.close() 939 ``` 940 941 For anyone wondering why the clients don't create a 0-byte file in the `create()` call, 942 it would cause problems after `close()` —the marker file could get 943 returned in `open()` calls instead of the final data. 944 945 #### Visibility of the output of a stream after `close()` 946 947 One guarantee which Object Stores SHOULD make is the same as those of POSIX 948 filesystems: After a stream `close()` call returns, the data MUST be persisted 949 durably and visible to all callers. Unfortunately, even that guarantee is 950 not always met: 951 952 1. Existing data on a path MAY be visible for an indeterminate period of time. 953 954 1. If the store has any form of create inconsistency or buffering of negative 955 existence probes, then even after the stream's `close()` operation has returned, 956 `getFileStatus(FS, path)` and `open(FS, path)` may fail with a `FileNotFoundException`. 957 958 In their favour, the atomicity of the store's PUT operations do offer their 959 own guarantee: a newly created object is either absent or all of its data 960 is present: the act of instantiating the object, while potentially exhibiting 961 create inconsistency, is atomic. Applications may be able to use that fact 962 to their advantage. 963 964 The [Abortable](abortable.html) interface exposes this ability to abort an output 965 stream before its data is made visible, so can be used for checkpointing and similar 966 operations. 967 968 ## Implementors notes. 969 970 ### Always implement `Syncable` -even if just to throw `UnsupportedOperationException` 971 972 Because `FSDataOutputStream` silently downgrades `Syncable.hflush()` 973 and `Syncable.hsync()` to `wrappedStream.flush()`, callers of the 974 API MAY be misled into believing that their data has been flushed/synced 975 after syncing to a stream which does not support the APIs. 976 977 Implementations SHOULD implement the API but 978 throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. 979 980 ### `StreamCapabilities` 981 982 Implementors of filesystem clients SHOULD implement the `StreamCapabilities` 983 interface and its `hasCapabilities()` method to to declare whether or not 984 an output streams offer the visibility and durability guarantees of `Syncable`. 985 986 Implementors of `StreamCapabilities.hasCapabilities()` MUST NOT declare that 987 they support the `hflush` and `hsync` capabilities on streams where this is not true. 988 989 Sometimes streams pass their data to store, but the far end may not 990 sync it all the way to disk. That is not something the client can determine. 991 Here: if the client code is making the hflush/hsync passes these requests 992 on to the distributed FS, it SHOULD declare that it supports them. 993 994 ### Metadata updates 995 996 Implementors MAY NOT update a file's metadata (length, date, ...) after 997 every `hsync()` call. HDFS doesn't, except when the written data crosses 998 a block boundary. 999 1000 1001 1002 ### Does `close()` synchronize and persist data? 1003 1004 By default, HDFS does not immediately data to disk when a stream is closed; it will 1005 be asynchronously saved to disk. 1006 1007 This does not mean that users do not expect it. 1008 1009 The behavior as implemented is similar to the write-back aspect's of NFS's 1010 [caching](https://docstore.mik.ua/orelly/networking_2ndEd/nfs/ch07_04.htm). 1011 `DFSClient.close()` is performing an `hflush()` to the client to upload 1012 all data to the datanodes. 1013 1014 1. `close()` SHALL return once the guarantees of `hflush()` are met: the data is 1015 visible to others. 1016 1. For durability guarantees, `hsync()` MUST be called first.
